content: Penicillin G sodium should not be administered to patients who require less than one million units per dose. This is particularly important for pediatric patients, as outlined in the precautions section regarding pediatric use. In cases of renal impairment, Penicillin G is generally considered relatively non-toxic. However, dosage adjustments are typically necessary only in patients with severe renal impairment. For patients with a body surface area of 73 m², a full loading dose should be administered initially, followed by half of the loading dose every 8 to 10 hours. Alternatively, in some cases, the half-dose may need to be administered every 4 to 5 hours. Additional dosage modifications should be made for patients who have both hepatic disease and renal impairment. For most acute infections, treatment should continue for at least 48 to 72 hours after the patient becomes asymptomatic. In the case of Group A β-hemolytic streptococcal infections, antibiotic therapy must be maintained for a minimum of 10 days to reduce the risk of developing rheumatic fever. Before administering parenteral drug products, the solution and container should be visually inspected for particulate matter and discoloration whenever the solution and container allow for such inspection. To prepare solutions of Penicillin G, the following steps should be followed: First, loosen the powder in the vial. Hold the vial horizontally and rotate it while slowly directing the stream of diluent against the wall of the vial. Once all the diluent has been added, shake the vial vigorously to ensure proper mixing. Suitable diluents include 0.9% Sodium Chloride Injection, USP, or Dextrose Injections, USP. It is important to note that penicillins are rapidly inactivated in the presence of carbohydrate solutions at an alkaline pH.
